paragraphs: The great misfortune is that they both acquire manners before morals, and a knowledge of life before reflection has given them any acquaintance with the grand ideal outline of human nature. The result is only natural. Content with human nature as it commonly appears, they fall prey to prejudices; and since they take all their opinions on trust, they submit blindly to authority. So if they have any good sense, it is a sort of instinctive glance that takes in proportions and passes judgment on manners, but that fails whenever arguments must be pursued below the surface or opinions analysed.

May not the same remark be applied to women? Indeed, the argument may be pushed further still, for both are thrown out of any useful station by the unnatural distinctions established in civilized life. Riches and hereditary honours have turned women into ciphers, mere zeros that lend importance to the figure standing before them; and idleness has bred in society a mixture of gallantry and despotism which leads the very men who are slaves to their mistresses to tyrannize over their sisters, wives and daughters. This, it is true, merely keeps them in rank and file. Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and blind obedience will come to an end; but since power always seeks blind obedience, tyrants and sensualists are quite right to try to keep women in the dark, for the former want only slaves and the latter a plaything. The sensualist, indeed, has been the most dangerous of tyrants; and women have been duped by their lovers, as princes are by their ministers, while dreaming that they ruled over them.

I am now chiefly alluding to Rousseau, for his character of Sophia is undoubtedly a captivating one, though it strikes me as grossly unnatural. What I intend to attack, however, is not the superstructure but the foundation of her character: the principles on which her education was built. Indeed, warmly as I admire the genius of that able writer, whose opinions I shall often have occasion to cite, when I read his voluptuous reveries indignation always takes the place of admiration, and the stern frown of insulted virtue wipes away the smile of pleasure that his eloquent sentences usually raise. Is this the man who, in his ardour for virtue, would banish all the gentle arts of peace and almost carry us back to Spartan discipline? Is this the man who delights in painting the useful struggles of passion, the triumphs of good dispositions, and the heroic flights that carry the glowing soul beyond itself? How these mighty sentiments are lowered when he describes the pretty foot and enticing airs of his little favourite! But I set the subject aside for now; and, rather than severely rebuking the passing outpourings of overweening sensibility, I shall only observe that anyone who has looked on society with a benevolent eye must often have been gratified by the sight of humble mutual love, neither dignified by sentiment nor strengthened by shared intellectual pursuits. The domestic trifles of the day have supplied matter for cheerful talk, and innocent caresses have softened labours that called for no great exercise of mind or stretch of thought. Yet has not the sight of this modest happiness stirred more tenderness than respect? It is an emotion like the one we feel when children are playing or animals frolicking; whereas the contemplation of the noble struggles of suffering merit has raised our admiration and carried our thoughts to that world where sensation will give way to reason.
Women, therefore, must be regarded either as moral beings, or as so weak that they must be wholly subjected to the superior faculties of men.

Let us examine this question. Rousseau declares that a woman should never for a moment feel herself independent; that she should be ruled by fear so as to exercise her NATURAL cunning; and that she should be made a coquettish slave so that she may be a more alluring object of desire, a SWEETER companion to man whenever he chooses to relax. He pushes still further the arguments that he claims to draw from the indications of nature, and hints that truth and fortitude, the cornerstones of all human virtue, should be cultivated only within certain limits, because, where the female character is concerned, obedience is the great lesson that must be impressed with unrelenting rigour.

What nonsense! When will some great man appear with strength of mind enough to blow away the fumes with which pride and sensuality have clouded this subject! If women are inferior to men by nature, their virtues must nonetheless be of the same quality, if not of the same degree, or else virtue becomes a merely relative idea; it follows that their conduct ought to rest on the same principles and aim at the same goal.

Bound to man as daughters, wives and mothers, women may have their moral character judged by the way they fulfil those simple duties; but the end, the great end, of their efforts should be to unfold their own faculties and acquire the dignity of conscious virtue. They may try to make their road pleasant, but, like men, they ought never to forget that life does not yield the happiness that can satisfy an immortal soul. I do not mean to suggest that either sex should become so lost in abstract reflection or distant prospects as to forget the affections and duties that lie before them, which are in truth the means appointed to produce the fruit of life. On the contrary, I would warmly recommend them, even while I assert that they give the most satisfaction when they are seen in their true, subordinate light.

The prevailing opinion that woman was created for man may well have originated in Moses’s poetic story. Yet since very few people, one presumes, who have given the subject any serious thought have ever supposed that Eve was literally one of Adam’s ribs, the inference must be allowed to collapse; or it may be admitted only so far as it proves that man, from the remotest antiquity, found it convenient to use his strength to subjugate his companion, and his ingenuity to show that her neck ought to be bent under the yoke, because she, like the brute creation, was created to do his pleasure.

Let no one conclude that I wish to turn the order of things upside down. I have already granted that, from the constitution of their bodies, men seem designed by Providence to attain a greater degree of virtue. I speak collectively of the whole sex; but I see not the shadow of a reason to conclude that their virtues should differ in nature. Indeed, how could they, if virtue has only one eternal standard? If I reason consistently, therefore, I must maintain as firmly that they have the same simple direction as that there is a God.

It follows, then, that cunning should not be set up against wisdom, petty cares against great exertions, or insipid softness, varnished over with the name of gentleness, against the fortitude that only grand views can inspire.

I shall be told that woman would then lose many of her particular graces, and the opinion of a well-known poet may be quoted to refute my unqualified assertions. For Pope has said, speaking for the whole male sex,
“Yet ne’er so sure our passions to create, As when she touch’d the brink of all we hate.”

I leave it to the judicious to decide in what light this sally places men and women; for the present I shall be content to observe that I cannot see why, unless they are mortal, females should always be degraded by being made subordinate to love or lust.

To speak disrespectfully of love is, I know, high treason against sentiment and fine feelings; but I wish to speak the plain language of truth, and to appeal to the head rather than the heart. Trying to reason love out of the world would be to outdo Cervantes in Quixotism, and would be just as great an offence against common sense; but an attempt to restrain this tumultuous passion, and to prove that it should not be allowed to dethrone the higher powers or to seize the sceptre that the understanding should always wield with composure, seems less wild.

In both sexes youth is the season for love; but during those days of thoughtless enjoyment, provision ought to be made for the weightier years of life, when sensation gives way to reflection. Yet Rousseau, and most of the male writers who have trodden in his footsteps, have warmly taught that the entire tendency of female education should be aimed at a single point: to make women pleasing.

Let me reason with those supporters of this opinion who have any knowledge of human nature: do they imagine that marriage can uproot the habits of a lifetime? The woman who has been taught only to please will soon find that her charms are slanting rays of sunlight, and that they can have little effect on her husband’s heart once they are seen every day, when summer is past and gone. Will she then have enough inner energy to look into herself for comfort and cultivate her dormant faculties? Or is it not more reasonable to expect that she will try to please other men, and, in the excitement raised by the hope of new conquests, try to forget the humiliation her love or pride has suffered? When the husband ceases to be a lover — and that time will inevitably come — her desire to please will then grow languid or turn into a source of bitterness; and love, perhaps the most fleeting of all passions, gives way to jealousy or vanity.

I am speaking now of women who are held back by principle or prejudice. Such women would shrink from an affair with real horror, yet they still wish to be persuaded, by the homage of gallant admirers, that their husbands cruelly neglect them; or they spend days and weeks dreaming of the happiness enjoyed by kindred souls, until their health is undermined and their spirits are broken by discontent. How, then, can the great art of pleasing be so necessary a study? It is useful only to a mistress. The chaste wife and serious mother should regard her power to please merely as the polish on her virtues, and her husband’s affection as one of the comforts that make her task less difficult and her life happier. But whether she is loved or neglected, her first wish should be to make herself worthy of respect, and not to rest all her happiness on a being subject to the same weaknesses as herself.
The amiable Dr. Gregory made a similar mistake. I respect his heart, but I wholly disapprove of his celebrated Legacy to his Daughters.
